newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia considered Laos bombing raids - papers.
newsitem.headline: Australia considered Laos bombing raids - papers.

text.p: Australia considered joining the United States in covert bombing raids in Laos during the Vietnam War, but decided against it because it feared it could not keep it secret, according to 1966 Australian Cabinet documents.

The documents, released on Wednesday by the Australian Archives under a 30-year secrecy rule, said the then Australian government of prime minister Harold Holt was under pressure from the United States to join the secret air war over neutral Laos.

The plan put to Australia was for it to send its eight Sabre air force jets based at Ubon in Thailand on missions in support of U.S. raids against North Vietnamese supply lines, according to media reports of the Cabinet documents.
"The non-availability of our Sabres for operations in Laos could lead to an American request that we vacate the airstrip," said a secret Australian Defence Department report to Cabinet.
"On the other hand the United States flies these missions on a deniable basis which we would find difficult to sustain because we have no other Sabres deployed in the area," it said.
"It is likely that Australian operations in Laos would become known and since the aircraft must have operated from Thailand, this could affect our relations with both countries."
The United States made a formal approach to Australia join the raids in a letter dated December 1965 through General Hunter Harris, commander-in-chief of the U.S. Pacific Air Force.

Harris noted the rising deployment of air operations and suggested the Sabres at Ubon, which was being used by U.S. aircraft to raid Laos, be put "on alert for Laos armed with rockets or bombs and 30 mm (cannons)".
"In light of previous Thai and Lao acceptance of U.S. operations, it does not appear that political clearances will present any obstacles," General Harris said.
The Australian Cabinet considered the request in February 1966 as part of U.S. pressure to increase Australia's military commitment to Vietnam.
On March 2, the Australian government increased its troop commitment to 4,500 soldiers from an initial team of advisers in 1962 and an infantry battalion of 1,400 in 1965.
On the same day it also decided that no new air or navy contribution could be offered at that stage.
North Vietnam used Laotian territory as part of the Ho Chi Minh Trail to ship arms and supplies from north to south Vietnam.
U.S. air raids on the trail, as many as 300 a day, started in late 1964 when the United States decided it could shorten the war if it halted the flow of supplies.
